newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Senate rebukes Mexico on drugs, seeks reforms.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Senate rebukes Mexico on drugs, seeks reforms.

text.p: The Senate on Thursday approved legislation criticising Mexico's performance in the anti-drug war and listing goals for stepping up its efforts.

The joint resolution, approved 94-5, was a compromise drafted in cooperation with the Clinton administration, which had opposed a House of Representatives vote last week to overturn President Bill Clinton's finding that Mexico has fully cooperated in fighting drugs.
Clinton welcomed the Senate action in a statement issued in Helsinki where he was to have talks with Russian President Boris Yeltsin.
"The Senate and I share a common goal," Clinton said. "We both want to improve cooperation with Mexico."
Mexico, which was furious following the House vote last week, welcomed the Senate measure, which it said would help cooperation between both sides against illegal drugs.
"Reason, sensitivity and a desire to cooperate prevailed over sheer recrimination," Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria said in a prepared statement.
Clinton ruled on Feb. 28 that Mexico was a reliable ally in the war against drugs, a step required to spare it U.S. economic sanctions.
Congressional critics said Mexico did not merit such a declaration and the House voted to overturn it, suspending its rebuke for 90 days to give Mexico time to improve its record.

When Mexico threatened to react harshly to the House move, key senators began negotiations with administration officials who feared a harsh resolution would torpedo the very cooperation being sought from Mexico.
The result was a softer, largely symbolic, measure criticising inadequacies in the Mexican anti-drug effort and requiring Clinton to report by Sept. 1 on improvements.

Sen. Dianne Feinstein, a California Democrat and one of three senators leading the negotiations, told the Senate that inadequate progress by Mexico would leave "no alternative but to fuel up for another Mexico certification battle next year."
Opponents of the legislation argued that Clinton, by certifying a country that clearly was not cooperating fully, had failed to abide by the law.
Voting against the measure were Republicans Sam Brownback of Kansas, Tim Hutchinson of Arkansas, Bob Smith of New Hampshire, Craig Thomas of Wyoming and Democrat Robert Torricelli of New Jersey.

The Senate measure listed a number of specific failures in Mexico's anti-drugs effort and concluded: "There has been ineffective and insufficient progress in halting the production and transit through Mexico of illegal drugs."

It said much of the cocaine used in the United States came from Mexico, there was evidence Mexican institutions were affected by "significant corruption" and Mexico has yet to fully implement new laws against organised crime and money laundering.
It said Mexican drug cartels operated with impunity and Mexico has not honoured any U.S. requests to extradite Mexican nationals indicted in the United states on drug charges.

The required presidential report would detail progress by the two governments on dismantling drug trafficking organisations, on strengthening bilateral cooperation and border enforcement and on denying safe havens to traffickers.
It would have to detail actions on crop eradication, money laundering and criminal screening of law enforcement officers.
The legislation called for information on progress by the United States in anti-drug education, international drug interdiction and deployment of 1,000 additional immigration patrol agents.
The resolution was expected to go to a Senate-House conference committee.
